claims.text: Slow annealing, relative to rapid quenching, increases short-range atomic ordering in nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs solid-solution catalysts.
Increasing short-range atomic ordering enhances selectivity toward complete ethanol oxidation and CO2 formation.
Increased atomic ordering creates defined active-site ensembles.
The defined active-site ensembles modify adsorption energies of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
The defined active-site ensembles modify activation barriers for ethanol oxidation.
Rapidly quenched nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs catalysts possess a comparatively random atomic arrangement.
TEM and EXAFS can be used to verify differences in atomic-level ordering and local ensemble configurations.
Changes in the distribution of active-site ensembles alter adsorption properties and reaction barriers.
Altered adsorption properties and reaction barriers shift ethanol oxidation from partial products toward complete oxidation to CO2.
The annealed catalyst is predicted to produce a higher proportion of CO2 than the rapidly quenched baseline.
The annealed catalyst is predicted to exhibit greater short-range atomic order than the rapidly quenched baseline.
The rapid-quench baseline favors partial oxidation of ethanol.
The proposed ordering-selectivity relationship is expected to hold at room temperature in alkaline electrolyte under steady-state potentials.
The ordering-selectivity effect may differ when temperature, pH, or applied potential range is significantly changed.
Annealing may concurrently change morphology or surface area, confounding attribution of selectivity changes to atomic ordering.
The experiment compares slow-annealed and rapidly quenched catalysts under otherwise identical ethanol-oxidation conditions.
A lack of statistically significant improvement in CO2 selectivity after annealing would falsify the proposed hypothesis.
Evidence that selectivity changes correlate with surface-area or composition changes rather than ordering would refute the claimed ordering-specific mechanism.
